props.title: Le Jour Se Lève
props.initialSlug: Tragic love spiral leads factory worker to murder

sections.content: **Le Jour Se Lève** (1939) stands as a masterpiece of French poetic realism, with Jean Gabin delivering one of cinema's most powerful performances as François, a factory worker barricaded in his room after committing murder. Director Marcel Carné and screenwriter Jacques Prévert craft a devastating portrait of working-class tragedy through innovative flashback structure - a technique that influenced film noir and inspired **The Killers** (1946) and **D.O.A.** (1950). The film's claustrophobic atmosphere and fatalistic tone exemplify poetic realism's dark romanticism, while its examination of class struggle and doomed love resonates with earlier works like **Pépé le Moko** (1937). movies.slug: A factory worker barricades himself in his apartment after killing a man, reflecting on the events that led him there

sections.content: The film's influence on American film noir cannot be overstated. The trapped protagonist narrating his downfall through flashbacks became a noir staple, seen in Double Indemnity (1944) and **Sunset Boulevard** (1950). Carné's expressionistic lighting and composition, achieved with cinematographer Philippe Agostini, created a visual template for noir's signature style. The social commentary - particularly regarding class mobility and industrial working conditions - connects to later neo-realist works like **Bicycle Thieves** (1948).

The central performance by Jean Gabin defines the "tragic romantic hero" archetype that would influence generations of actors. His François is both tender and volatile, a working-class everyman destroyed by forces beyond his control. This characterization echoes through **On the Waterfront** (1954) and even modern films like **Drive** (2011), where Ryan Gosling's stoic driver recalls Gabin's contained intensity. sections.content: While banned during the Nazi occupation of France for its "demoralizing" influence, **Le Jour Se Lève** (1939) emerged as a cornerstone of humanitarian cinema. Its influence extends beyond noir to the French New Wave, where directors like Jean-Luc Godard referenced it in **Breathless** (1960). The film's psychological realism and social consciousness influenced Italian Neorealism, particularly **Rome, Open City** (1945), and later European art cinema like **The Conformist** (1970).
